title: Programming for people with limited mobility
summary: NH explains how novices, injured lifters and tall or oddly proportioned lifters can build robust mobility through programming. Open each day with heavy strength work in a comfortable range, then do a light, full-range mobility lift, usually an antagonist pattern. Over years the two ranges converge. The description includes a 4-day upper/lower template.
claims: Mobility is a spectrum and there's no objective standard everyone must meet; it depends on what you want your body to do
Mobility can be seen as robust rigidity: a pliable, resilient body that can endure positions
You don't have to develop mobility or squat ass-to-grass; be wary of people saying you must do things one way
Not squatting to depth isn't harmful to health, but learning it can be better for long-term muscle building and injury prevention
Lower body mobility matters most because squats and deadlifts put the spine at risk, while bad benching just hurts a shoulder
Many people who believe they'll never squat or deadlift properly again are wrong; the body re-adapts with time
Novices lack robust mobility simply because they never practiced; everyone can squat to depth and hip hinge, it's innate
Poor ankle mobility and collapsing ankles cause knee and lower back problems up the chain; fix it early
After a big accident or serious condition you need proper rehab, not training advice
He has scoliosis and had to work around it
Tall lifters aren't suited to most lifts as usually performed, but still want mobility adapted to their needs
Program two lift types: heavy lifts suited to your body for progressive overload, and light lifts for pushing mobility limits
Mobility is a muscular skill; going down and up comfortably relies on muscle memory and strength in that range
Use light weight for end-range mobility work, so a form breakdown doesn't cause tendon damage
If the bottom of the deadlift is a problem, pull from blocks or a rack at a height where you can keep a neutral back; never cat-back pull from the floor
For squats, try high bar, low bar, SSB, Zercher, play with stance, then squat to the depth where knees don't collapse, back doesn't round and butt wink is minimal, even if above parallel
Novices should squat without a box even if they can't hit depth, so they learn to squat unsupported
He likes beginners to start deadlifting in a rack to learn the hip hinge
Follow the strength lift with an antagonist pattern (knee flexion then hip hinge), performed with exaggerated, as-deep-as-possible range and light weight
Structural integrity comes mostly from weight selection, not technique: perfect form at 400 lb can become garbage at 450
Normies can reach depth but on their toes: they have mobility but not robust mobility
Increase strength-lift range incrementally; don't jump from parallel to ass-to-grass with the same load because light weight went well
You may hit a structural limit in range, and that's fine; each gained inch is tonnage and muscle
Mobility work protects you when a failed squat forces you to depth or peer pressure gets you pulling from the floor
Skipping floor deadlifts or deep squats leaves posterior chain, quad, glute and hamstring gains on the table
Ignore the form police and dogma; only increase range if you want it, and do it slowly
Mobility lifts keep a fixed max range and progress only in load; strength lifts progress in load and range until the two meet
Building robust mobility can take years, even 5-7 years after serious injury
He likes novices doing variations because they let them reach deeper ranges in most lifts
Template: 4-day upper/lower, each day opening with a comfortable-ROM strength lift (3x6-10, deadlift 3x4-6), then a full-ROM low-weight lift (3-4 sets) supersetted with pulls, then accessories
exercises: start at a height where you can keep a neutral back
skip the bottom range you can't control
depth where knees don't cave, back doesn't round, minimal butt wink
